studies.title: Not Created In Play
studies.meaning: An objection is quoted and then answered from two directions. The objection sets its own terms for proof: bring back our ancestors. The first answer is historical and points at a kingdom stronger than theirs that is no longer there. The second is structural and much larger. The heavens and the earth were not made in play. The commentators read that word precisely, since it names activity with no purpose beyond its own performance, so the argument is that a pointless universe is the assumption hidden inside the denial.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The people named here were the Himyarite kingdom of south Arabia, whose rulers carried that title, and their cities and inscriptions were known to Arabian traders. Naming them rather than a distant empire put the argument within reach of the objectors, who could ask their own caravans about the place. The Quran mentions them in only one other passage, in a similar list.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to unfold or spread something that was rolled, used of opening a scroll. Resurrection is pictured as a thing unfurled rather than reassembled from parts.
Not a personal name but the title borne by rulers of a south Arabian kingdom, in the way other peoples are named here by their king. The Quran uses it in only two places.
Activity with no purpose beyond its own doing. The word is not dismissive of games; it names the absence of an end outside the act, which is exactly the claim being denied.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The winter caravan went south to Yemen, and the road passed the remains of the old south Arabian kingdoms: the great broken dam, terraced fields gone dry, inscriptions in a script Meccans could see and not read. Merchants dealt with the region every year and knew its history as commercial knowledge rather than legend. A reference to that people pointed at something the audience had walked past.
studies.didYouKnow: The people named in this passage appear in only one other place in the whole Quran, again in a list of earlier communities that rejected their messengers. The Quran identifies them by a royal title rather than by a personal or tribal name, which is in fact how the rulers of that south Arabian kingdom were designated in their own inscriptions.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument runs from purpose rather than from power. Instead of asserting that God is able to raise the dead, the passage asks what kind of world the denial requires, and names it as play. That reverses the direction of the question: a reckoning is presented as the thing that makes the whole arrangement coherent rather than as an extra claim added on top of it. The next ayah states the same point positively.

crossReferences.why: Contains the only other mention of the same people, again among those who denied their messengers.
States the same denial about the heavens and the earth, and adds what would follow had it been otherwise.
Puts the argument as a direct question about the reader: did you suppose you were created for nothing?

studies.applyIt: Spend five minutes writing what you would do differently tomorrow if you were certain the arrangement had a purpose. Then look at your list and mark the items you could do anyway, regardless of what you are certain of. Most people find the list barely changes. That gap is what this passage is actually about.
